introduction-no-right-answers.core: System design interviews are open-ended: there's no single correct architecture, only trade-offs. Interviewers assess how you clarify requirements, estimate scale, choose components and justify trade-offs (consistency vs availability, cost vs latency) and how you respond to probing.

first_principles.problem: Candidates jump straight to drawing Kafka and Cassandra without asking what the system must do.
truths: Communication is part of the evaluation.

analogy.title: An architect meeting a client
analogy.story: You ask about family size, budget and lifestyle before sketching a house.
analogy.breaks: Houses take months to build; you have 45 minutes, so time management matters.

example.title: Designing a URL shortener
flow: Ask: reads vs writes? custom aliases? expiry?

check.q: What should you do first in a system design interview?
check.a: Clarify functional and non-functional requirements and scope.

back-of-the-envelope-math-powers-of-2.core: Quick estimates decide architecture: requests per second, storage per year and bandwidth. Use powers of 2 (2¹⁰ ≈ 1 thousand, 2²⁰ ≈ 1 million, 2³⁰ ≈ 1 billion), 1 day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ 10⁵ s, and round aggressively. The goal is the order of magnitude, not precision.

first_principles.problem: Without numbers, a candidate can't tell if one database suffices or a sharded cluster is needed.
truths: Orders of magnitude drive design choices.

analogy.title: Estimating how many pizzas to order for a party
analogy.story: Guests × slices each ÷ slices per pizza, rounded up, with no spreadsheet needed.
analogy.breaks: Pizza demand is steady; traffic has peaks and spikes.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.detail: Object storage needed; metadata DB handles 300 writes/s easily.

check.q: How many requests per second is 1 billion per day?

latency-numbers-what-is-slow.core: Know the rough latency ladder: L1 cache ~1 ns, RAM ~100 ns, SSD random read ~100 µs, same-datacenter round trip ~0.5 ms, HDD seek ~10 ms, cross-continent round trip ~100–150 ms. Each step is about 10–1,000× slower, which explains why caching and locality dominate design.

first_principles.problem: A design makes 50 sequential cross-region calls per request and wonders why p99 is 6 seconds.
derivation: **Avoid** cross-region hops on the hot path.

analogy.title: Fetching ingredients
analogy.story: Grabbing salt from the counter (cache), the pantry (RAM), the corner shop (SSD) or flying abroad (cross-continent).
analogy.breaks: You'd never fly abroad for salt, yet a design can do it accidentally with one remote call.

example.title: Budgeting a 200 ms request
flow: Cache hot keys in RAM: 0.1 ms

check.q: Roughly how much slower is a cross-continent round trip than a RAM read?
check.a: About a million times (≈100 ms vs ≈100 ns).

the-4-step-framework.core: A reliable structure: (1) clarify requirements and scope, (2) estimate scale and define APIs and data model, (3) draw a high-level design, (4) deep dive into bottlenecks, scaling and failure modes, then wrap up with trade-offs. It keeps 45 minutes on track and shows senior thinking.

first_principles.problem: Candidates spend 30 minutes on database schema and never discuss scaling or failures.
truths: Interviewers need signal on breadth and depth.

analogy.title: A pilot's flight plan
analogy.story: Pre-flight checks, take-off, cruise, then handling turbulence and landing.
analogy.breaks: Flights rarely change destination; interviewers may change requirements mid-way.

example.title: Applying it to a chat app
flow: Design: WebSocket gateways, message service, store
Deep dive: fan-out for groups, ordering, offline delivery

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Breadth and depth within the time.

check.q: What belongs in the deep-dive step?
check.a: Bottlenecks, scaling strategies, failure modes and detailed component design.

scaling-concepts-the-toolkit.core: Scaling tools: vertical then horizontal scaling, stateless services behind load balancers, caching (CDN, Redis), read replicas, sharding/partitioning, async processing with queues, denormalisation, and replication with CAP trade-offs. Each solves a specific bottleneck.

first_principles.problem: The database is the bottleneck, and the candidate's only answer is 'add more servers'.

analogy.title: Expanding a restaurant
analogy.story: More waiters (stateless), a prep station (cache), more kitchens (shards) and a ticket rail (queue).
analogy.breaks: Kitchens don't need consistency; shards and replicas must handle data correctness.

example.title: Scaling a read-heavy API
flow: Writes still fine → no sharding yet

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Fix the actual bottleneck, cheapest first.

check.q: Which technique scales writes beyond one database?
